b: Nature: Malignant — second most common malignant bone tumor in children
Who: Children and adolescents, 5–20 years. Rare in Black Africans
Where: Diaphysis of long bones — femur most common. Also flat bones (pelvis, ribs, scapula)
Histology: Small round blue cells — sheets of uniform small cells. Looks similar to lymphoma, neuroblastoma
Genetics: t(11;22) translocation — EWS-FLI1 fusion gene

es.q: Outline the defining histological, genetic, and clinical features of Ewing sarcoma.
es.m:
**Age and Cellular Appearance**
- Ewing sarcoma occurs primarily in adolescents.
- It is composed of small round blue cells, which are very immature-looking cells with little cytoplasm.
**Genetic Translocation**
- It is defined by a specific translocation, t(11;22) EWS-FLI1.
**Immunohistochemistry**
- Tumour cells test positive for the CD99 marker.

exam: What is the most specific diagnostic test for Ewing sarcoma? — Histology plus confirmation of EWS‑FLI1 fusion by cytogenetics or RT‑PCR.
Which imaging finding would most strongly suggest Ewing sarcoma over osteosarcoma? — Onion‑skin periosteal reaction on X‑ray.
A child presents with a painful, enlarging femoral diaphyseal mass and normal WBC. What is the next best step? — Obtain a core biopsy for histology and cytogenetics.
What is the first-line chemotherapy regimen for localized Ewing sarcoma? — Vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, etoposide (VDC/IE).
Why should doxorubicin be avoided in a patient with pre‑existing heart disease? — It is cardiotoxic and can worsen heart failure.
A patient with Ewing sarcoma develops a pathological fracture. What is the priority management? — Stabilise the fracture surgically and continue systemic chemotherapy.
ai.title: Ewing Sarcoma
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A malignant bone tumour of children, characterised by small round blue cells and a t(11;22) translocation. It presents with pain and swelling, often mimicking infection or other tumours.

b: Small round blue cells on H&E
sections.p: Ewing sarcoma is a small round blue cell tumour of bone, most common in the diaphysis of long bones in children and adolescents. Diagnosis requires histology and confirmation of the EWS‑FLI1 fusion by cytogenetics or RT‑PCR.

t.b: Shows an aggressive, permeative lesion with onion‑skin periosteal reaction – suggests Ewing over osteosarcoma
Defines tumour extent and marrow involvement – useful for surgical planning
Detects multifocal disease or occult lesions
Provides tissue for histology and cytogenetics – essential for diagnosis
Confirms EWS‑FLI1 fusion – definitive diagnosis

sections.p: Staging follows the International Society of Paediatric Oncology (SIOP) system: Stage I (localized), Stage II (regional nodes), Stage III (distant metastases). Prognosis worsens with metastasis and large tumour size.

t.b: Detects pulmonary metastases – most common site
Identifies skeletal spread

sections.p: The primary driver is the t(11;22) translocation creating an oncogenic fusion protein. Other factors include viral oncogenes and environmental exposures, but these are rare.

t.b: Can worsen prognosis but not a direct cause
May mimic presentation but not etiologic

sections.p: Patients report insidious pain, swelling, and sometimes fever. The pain is often worse at night and may be mistaken for infection or fracture.

t.b: Swelling, tenderness, limited ROM – differentiates from simple fracture by lack of callus

sections.p: A stepwise approach: imaging, biopsy, and molecular testing. In low‑resource settings, plain X‑ray and biopsy may be all that is available.

t.b: Shows permeative lesion with onion‑skin periosteal reaction – suggests Ewing over osteosarcoma

sections.p: Rapidly enlarging mass, pathological fracture, systemic symptoms, or new neurological deficits indicate aggressive disease or complications.

t.b: Detects spinal cord compression – urgent decompression needed

sections.p: Multimodal: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgery or radiotherapy, then adjuvant chemotherapy. Chemotherapy regimens use vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide.

t.b: Neurotoxic – avoid in pre‑existing neuropathy
Cardiotoxic – monitor ECG
Nephrotoxic – ensure hydration

sections.p: Regular imaging every 3–6 months for 2–3 years, then annually. Prevention focuses on early detection of bone pain and prompt investigation.
